opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I chose that name, I was trying to capture two things I think are central to where AI is now, and the relationship between them.

"Language" is the part we've made remarkable progress on. Large language models showed that if you train on enough human text, you get something with surprisingly general abilities: reasoning, coding, writing, even a kind of common sense. Language is humanity's compressed record of how we think and how we describe the world. So in a sense, language models inherited a huge amount of human prior knowledge for free.

"World" is the harder, more open-ended part. Language describes the world, but it isn't the world. When an agent actually has to act, whether by browsing a website, writing and running code, or operating in some physical or digital environment, it gets feedback that isn't just more text. It finds out whether its actions worked. That loop of acting, observing, and adjusting is where I think a lot of the next progress will come from.

What I find distinctive, and what I wanted the name to signal, is that I don't see these as two separate research directions. The interesting question is how they connect. Can language serve as the interface through which an agent reasons about and acts in the world? Can experience in the world flow back and improve what the model understands? Much of the field has been focused on scaling language, or on building world models in a more perceptual, simulation-based way. I'm most interested in the space between them: language as a tool for thinking and acting, and the world as the source of grounding and of new data once we've exhausted what humans have already written down.

It's also a statement about evaluation and what we value. If models only live in language, it's easy to measure them on exam-style benchmarks. But the real test is whether they can do useful things in real environments, over long horizons, with real consequences. So "Language and World" is partly a reminder to myself to keep the research pointed at that.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as a major source of progress and says it is interested in connecting language and the world, but it does not say that viewing language as a carrier of intelligence shifted from a distinctive perspective to a broadly accepted one.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention 2014–2015 or explain that vision was then the prevailing priority.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say the name itself is the thesis. "Language" and "World" are the two things we think an intelligent agent fundamentally has to deal with, and the interesting part is the relationship between them.

For most of my research, going back to the work on ReAct and tree-of-thought and later the agent benchmarks, the question I kept circling was: a language model is very good at manipulating language, but how does it actually touch the world? Reasoning in text alone is a closed loop. You can produce beautiful chains of thought that are entirely wrong, because nothing ever pushed back. The world pushes back. When an agent runs a command, browses a page, or calls an API, it gets feedback that is not generated by itself, and that is where learning and grounding actually happen. So "language and world" is really about that interface: language as the medium of thought and planning, the world as the source of truth and reward.

The second part is "Studio," and that was deliberate. I didn't want to call it a lab. A lab suggests one principal investigator, graduate students, a pipeline of papers. A studio suggests craft, taste, and building things that people actually use. I think we're at a moment where the gap between a research idea and a product that millions of people touch has collapsed to almost nothing. The most important research results in agents right now are not really coming out as papers. They're coming out as systems where someone has thought carefully about the environment, the tools, the reward signal, and the user experience all at once. A studio is the structure that lets you treat those as one problem instead of four.

And the third thing, which I think makes the perspective a bit different from the mainstream, is that we care a lot about environments, not just models. The industry spends most of its energy on making the model bigger or the training recipe better. I think the bottleneck has shifted. The models are already capable enough that what limits them is the quality and diversity of worlds we give them to act in. Designing the right environment, the right task, the right feedback, is itself the research. If you get that right, the model learns what it needs to. If you get it wrong, no amount of scaling fixes it.

So, distinctiveness in one sentence: we're less interested in what a model can say and more interested in what it can do, and we think the way you find that out is by building worlds and putting agents in them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language as a medium for thought and planning, but does not describe a shift from that view being distinctive to becoming broadly accepted.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention 2014–2015 or explain that vision was the prevailing priority when language’s role in intelligence was distinctive.

astra-6.text:
我觉得“语言”和“世界”放在一起，最有意思的是它们之间的关系。语言让我们能够描述世界、交流知识，甚至构造一些现实中还不存在的东西。但语言又不是世界本身。你能把一件事情讲得很清楚，不一定意味着你真的能把它做好。

放到人工智能上，这就对应着一个我很关心的问题：模型在语言里学到了很多东西，这些能力怎么才能变成它在真实环境里解决问题的能力？当它采取一个行动，环境会给它反馈，而且这个反馈不一定符合它原来的预期。它需要根据反馈调整自己，而不只是继续生成一段听起来合理的话。

所以我会把这个名字理解成一种双向的视角：既看语言如何帮助我们理解和改变世界，也看世界如何检验、修正我们在语言里形成的认识。我觉得独特的地方可能就在于，不把表达能力当作终点，而是继续追问：它和实际发生的事情之间，到底是什么关系？

r001.rationale: The response discusses language as a way to describe the world and contrasts expression with real-world ability, but does not say that seeing language as a carrier of intelligence shifted from distinctive to broadly accepted.

r002.rationale: It does not mention 2014–2015 or the prevailing view that prioritized vision.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the interesting part is the relationship between language and the world. Language lets us describe things, share knowledge, and reason, but it isn’t the whole world. There are things you only discover by acting, observing what happens, and adjusting your understanding.

That also shapes how I think about AI. We can ask whether a model produces a good answer, but we can also ask whether it can use that answer to do something, learn from feedback, and make progress on a task. That moves our attention from language as an output to language as part of an interaction with the world.

And I like the word “studio” because it suggests making things and experimenting. You build something, see where your understanding breaks down, and then return to the underlying questions. To me, that back-and-forth is the distinctive perspective.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as part of interaction with the world, but does not say that viewing language as an important carrier of intelligence shifted from distinctive to broadly accepted.

r002.rationale: It gives no 2014–2015 timeframe and does not mention that vision was the prevailing priority.
